stem:
You are the psychiatric registrar consulted urgently to the emergency department to see a 42 year old man with schizophrenia who has been unwell for 3 days.

He was reviewed 2 weeks ago in the community clinic and had his depot flupenthixol dose increased. He was also commenced on olanzapine 10 mg orally at night to help with breakthrough symptoms. He takes no other medications. He has no known allergies.

In the cubicle he is confused and diaphoretic. Muscle tone is markedly increased with lead pipe rigidity in all four limbs. Reflexes are 2+ without clonus. Pupils are equal and reactive. Bowel sounds are present.

Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 168/98, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 40.1. Creatine kinase 12 400 U/L (30-190). Sodium 138, potassium 4.0, creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-120), lactate 3.2 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 168/98, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 40.1
data_table.Neuromuscular: Lead pipe rigidity all four limbs; reflexes 2+; no clonus; pupils equal reactive; bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: CK 12 400 U/L (30-190); creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-120); lactate 3.2 mmol/L; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Recent changes: Depot flupenthixol dose increased 2 weeks ago; olanzapine 10 mg nightly commenced same visit

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate first specific intervention?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: cease all antipsychotics, transfer to intensive care for aggressive cooling and supportive care
options.rationale: The clinical picture, hyperthermia, lead pipe rigidity, dysautonomia, and grossly elevated creatine kinase after recent antipsychotic escalation is NMS; first line is cessation of the offending drug and supportive care in a high acuity setting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Antipsychotic use in schizophrenia).

options.text: Serotonin syndrome: cease all serotonergic agents, give cyproheptadine 12 mg orally, and admit to a monitored bed
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia and inducible clonus rather than lead pipe rigidity, and there is no serotonergic drug in the history to precipitate it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Anticholinergic delirium: cease all antipsychotics, give physostigmine 1 mg intravenous, and admit to a monitored bed
options.rationale: Anticholinergic delirium presents with mydriasis, absent bowel sounds, and dry skin; his diaphoresis and normal pupils argue against it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia: cease all antipsychotics, commence dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenous, and transfer to intensive care
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetic or succinylcholine, neither of which he has received (Source: ANZCA Malignant Hyperthermia Resource Kit).

options.text: Acute dystonic reaction: cease all antipsychotics, give benztropine 2 mg intramuscular, and admit for observation
options.rationale: Acute dystonia produces focal muscle spasm rather than generalised rigidity with hyperthermia and dysautonomia; benztropine does not treat NMS (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Recent antipsychotic dose escalation with hyperthermia, lead pipe rigidity, dysautonomia, and a creatine kinase in the thousands is classic NMS. Serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia and clonus, not lead pipe rigidity, and requires a serotonergic precipitant. Anticholinergic delirium has mydriasis and absent bowel sounds. Cease antipsychotics and support in ICU; consider dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe or refractory cases.
key_points: NMS lead pipe rigidity contrasts with serotonin syndrome hyperreflexia and clonus.
CK is grossly elevated in NMS.
First step is cessation of the offending drug and supportive intensive care.
explanation.pearls: Lead pipe rigidity plus hyperthermia plus CK in the thousands after antipsychotic escalation is NMS, not serotonin syndrome; the latter demands a serotonergic precipitant and hyperreflexia.

stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia stabilised on clozapine 400 mg orally at night for 3 years. He attends monthly clozapine monitoring bloods without missed reviews.

Today's full blood count reports a neutrophil count of 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5) with a total white cell count of 3.1 x10^9/L and normal haemoglobin and platelets. His previous monthly counts have been within normal limits. He is otherwise well, has no fever or infective symptoms, and has not travelled overseas recently.

He asks whether he needs to stop his clozapine today.

data_table.Clozapine dose: 400 mg orally at night for 3 years without dose change
data_table.Bloods today: Neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); WCC 3.1 x10^9/L; haemoglobin and platelets within normal limits
data_table.Symptoms: No fever; no infective symptoms; no recent overseas travel

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step according to the Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and admit for haematology review because neutrophils below 1.5 x10^9/L represent the red zone
options.rationale: The Australian red zone is neutrophils below 1.0 x10^9/L; 1.2 x10^9/L is amber, in which the drug is continued with intensified monitoring (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat full blood count twice weekly until neutrophils return above 1.5 x10^9/L
options.rationale: The Australian clozapine amber zone is neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L, in which clozapine continues with twice weekly full blood counts until recovery above 1.5 x10^9/L (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols; TGA clozapine product information).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.text: Reduce clozapine dose by 50% and repeat the count in 2 weeks with return to standard monthly monitoring
options.rationale: Dose reduction is not part of the amber zone protocol; monitoring is intensified rather than the dose changed (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and continue monthly monitoring because the patient is asymptomatic
options.rationale: Being asymptomatic does not remove the amber zone requirement to intensify monitoring; monthly counts are inadequate at this neutrophil level (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.text: Give filgrastim 300 microgram subcutaneous today to raise neutrophils before further blood counts are taken
options.rationale: Granulocyte colony stimulating factor is reserved for red zone counts and clozapine rechallenge decisions in specialist settings rather than routine amber zone management (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

explanation.summary: Australian clozapine monitoring uses a three zone system: green (neutrophils 1.5 x10^9/L or above), amber (1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L), and red (below 1.0 x10^9/L). In the amber zone the drug is continued but the count is repeated twice weekly until recovery. Dose reduction and colony stimulating factor are not part of the amber zone response.
key_points: Amber zone: neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L; continue drug; twice weekly counts.
Red zone: neutrophils below 1.0 x10^9/L; cease clozapine and refer.
Filgrastim is reserved for red zone or specialist rechallenge.
explanation.pearls: The Australian clozapine amber zone (neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L) is managed by continuing clozapine and repeating full blood count twice weekly until neutrophils recover above 1.5 x10^9/L.

sources.label: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

stem:
You are the emergency registrar at a regional hospital 90 minutes drive by road from the nearest primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) capable centre. Helicopter retrieval is available and current wait for retrieval is 30 minutes on the ground.

A 58 year old man presents 45 minutes into ongoing central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm. He has a background of hypertension and hyperlipidaemia; he smokes 15 cigarettes a day. He has no history of stroke, no recent surgery, and no anticoagulation.

On assessment he is diaphoretic. Chest is clear on auscultation. There is no murmur.

Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 148/86, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.6. Twelve lead ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in leads V1 to V4 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III, and aVF. High sensitivity troponin is pending. Aspirin 300 mg oral and ticagrelor 180 mg oral have been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 148/86, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.ECG: 3 mm ST elevation V1 to V4; reciprocal ST depression II, III, aVF
data_table.Time course: Chest pain onset 45 minutes ago; ongoing
data_table.Access to PCI: Primary PCI centre 90 minutes by road; helicopter retrieval available with 30 minute ground wait
data_table.Antiplatelets given: Aspirin 300 mg PO and ticagrelor 180 mg PO
data_table.Bleeding risk: No stroke; no recent surgery; not on anticoagulation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Give a heparin bolus alone and admit for troponin trend before deciding whether or how to reperfuse the patient
options.rationale: ST elevation meeting STEMI criteria mandates immediate reperfusion; awaiting troponin delays therapy without changing the diagnosis (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Transfer by helicopter for primary PCI at the tertiary centre and delay any reperfusion drug until after arrival
options.rationale: Waiting to reach primary PCI when the total time is likely to exceed 120 minutes from first medical contact adds ischaemic time; fibrinolysis at the regional site is preferred (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Administer intravenous tenecteplase now and transfer to the PCI capable centre for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails
options.rationale: CSANZ recommends fibrinolysis when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact; expected door in to balloon time here exceeds 120 minutes, so tenecteplase now with transfer for rescue PCI is preferred (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Give intravenous morphine 5 mg and glyceryl trinitrate infusion; defer reperfusion pending haemodynamic stability
options.rationale: Analgesia and nitrate infusion are supportive but must not defer reperfusion in STEMI (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange non urgent invasive coronary angiography within 72 hours after risk stratification with a stress echocardiogram
options.rationale: Delayed angiography is appropriate for stable NSTEMI at intermediate risk, not for STEMI where time critical reperfusion is mandatory (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

explanation.summary: STEMI with expected PCI delay over 120 minutes from first medical contact is treated with fibrinolysis at the regional site (tenecteplase weight based) followed by transfer to a PCI centre for review. Rescue PCI applies when there is failure of reperfusion at 90 minutes with persistent ST elevation or ongoing pain. Primary PCI is preferred only when it can be achieved within the 120 minute window from first medical contact.
key_points: PCI within 120 minutes preferred; otherwise fibrinolysis.
Rescue PCI after failed fibrinolysis (persistent ST elevation, ongoing pain).
Do not defer reperfusion for troponin results.
explanation.pearls: STEMI at a regional site more than 120 minutes from primary PCI is fibrinolysis now with transfer for rescue PCI, not helicopter transfer without reperfusion.

stem:
You are the acute medicine registrar. A 27 year old man with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections presents with 24 hours of vomiting, deep breathing, and abdominal pain. He ran out of his rapid acting insulin 2 days ago.

On assessment he is alert but drowsy. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Mucous membranes are dry.

Vital signs: pulse 122, blood pressure 106/64, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.4. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L. Sodium 134, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, chloride 100, urea 9, creatinine 118 micromol/L. He weighs 80 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 106/64, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Alert but drowsy; cool peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 134, potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 100, urea 9, creatinine 118 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 100 mL bolus because the venous pH is currently under 7.15
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only considered for severe acidaemia with pH under 6.9 in adults; it is not indicated at pH 7.10 (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 2 L bolus over 15 minutes then commence 5% dextrose 250 mL/hour before starting insulin
options.rationale: A 2 L rapid bolus over 15 minutes is not standard in adult DKA without shock; dextrose is added when glucose falls to 12 to 14 mmol/L (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: Commence insulin infusion at 0.14 unit/kg/hour immediately without any preceding fluid load or bolus
options.rationale: Insulin without volume resuscitation shifts potassium intracellularly, worsens hypoperfusion, and increases arrhythmia risk (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 60 minutes, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour after the first bag
options.rationale: The ADS DKA pathway gives 1 L 0.9% saline over the first hour and starts a fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour; add potassium once serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: Give a subcutaneous rapid acting insulin bolus of 10 units before commencing any intravenous fluid or infusion
options.rationale: Subcutaneous rapid insulin has unpredictable absorption in shock or dehydration; intravenous infusion is preferred alongside fluid resuscitation (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

explanation.summary: This is adult DKA without frank shock. ADS treats with 1 L 0.9% saline over the first hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour, with potassium added once serum K falls below 5.5 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is only considered when pH is below 6.9.
key_points: First hour: 0.9% saline 1 L in adult DKA.
Insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour after first bag.
Add potassium when serum K falls below 5.5 mmol/L; bicarbonate only if pH under 6.9.
explanation.pearls: The ADS adult DKA opening move is 1 L 0.9% saline over 1 hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour, with potassium added when serum K drops below 5.5 mmol/L.

sources.label: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

subtopic_detail: DOAC dose in non valvular AF with renal impairment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 78 year old woman with non valvular atrial fibrillation attends for review. She was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice daily 4 weeks ago at her cardiology appointment.

She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Repeat urea and electrolytes today show creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-100) and eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. She weighs 62 kg. She has no active bleeding.

She takes perindopril 4 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and empagliflozin 10 mg daily. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 5.

data_table.Current dose: Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily for 4 weeks
data_table.Renal function: Creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-100); eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m2; potassium 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Other conditions: Hypertension; type 2 diabetes; stage 3b CKD; CHA2DS2-VA 5
data_table.Other medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily; metformin 1 g twice daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; empagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to her apixaban dose?

options.text: Cease anticoagulation because CHA2DS2-VA 5 is offset by bleeding risk at this age
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA 5 confers a substantial stroke risk that outweighs bleeding risk in most patients and warrants continued anticoagulation (Source: CSANZ Australian AF Guidelines).

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg orally twice daily because her creatinine is at or above 133 micromol/L
options.rationale: A single criterion is insufficient for dose reduction; two of three (age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above) are required (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

options.text: Switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3 because eGFR under 50 mL/min contraindicates apixaban
options.rationale: Apixaban is not contraindicated at eGFR 34 mL/min; it remains preferred over warfarin in most patients with CrCl above 25 mL/min in Australian practice (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

options.text: Switch to dabigatran 110 mg orally twice daily to reduce bleeding risk at this eGFR
options.rationale: Dabigatran is more renally cleared than apixaban and is not preferred at eGFR 34 mL/min without a specific indication (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Dabigatran).

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily because she meets only one of the three reduction criteria
options.rationale: Apixaban dose reduction to 2.5 mg BD requires two of age 80 years or above, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or above; she meets only the creatinine criterion so the standard 5 mg BD dose continues (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

explanation.summary: Apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BD only when two of three criteria are met: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or above. She meets only one criterion so the standard 5 mg BD dose continues. Anticoagulation is warranted with CHA2DS2-VA 5.
key_points: Apixaban dose reduction requires 2 of 3 criteria.
eGFR 34 mL/min is not itself an apixaban contraindication in Australia.
explanation.pearls: Apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BD only when at least 2 of 3 apply: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above.
